title: Slab-built hexagonal planter set in air-dry clay
subtitle: Three matching six-sided planters in graduated sizes, built from slabs
excerpt: Three hexagonal planters in small, medium, and large sizes built from air-dry clay slabs. The six-sided walls give a geometric look different from round pinch pots or rectangular slab boxes. Each planter holds a single small succulent or cactus in a nursery pot.
sourceNotes: Technique derived from first principles. Slab-building methods referenced from Encyclopedia Britannica 11th edition (1911) pottery entry.

glossaryTerms.definition: A flat sheet of clay rolled to an even thickness, used as the building unit
The drying stage where clay holds its shape but is still damp enough to join
Clay thinned with water, used to join clay pieces

content.text: A hexagonal planter requires cutting six identical rectangular wall panels and joining them at 120-degree angles. It sounds complex, but with a simple paper template it is a methodical
build. No kiln required. Suitable for dry-soil plants only.
Small planter: six walls 4 cm wide by 5 cm tall and a hexagonal base with 4 cm sides. Medium: six walls 5 cm by 6 cm. Large: six walls 6 cm by 7 cm. Roll all walls 6 mm thick.

Roll a slab 6 mm thick. Cut 18 rectangular wall panels in the three sets of six, using a metal ruler and fettling knife. Bevel the vertical edges of each panel to 30 degrees (half of 60 degrees per joint) using the fettling knife held at an angle, so the panels meet flush at 120 degrees when assembled.

Cut three hexagonal base pieces. To cut a hexagon, draw a circle of the correct radius on card, mark six equidistant points on the circumference with a protractor (60 degrees apart) and connect them. Use this template to cut the clay base.

Score all mating edges and apply

. Assemble the six wall panels around the hexagonal base one at a time, starting with two opposite panels and working around. Hold each join for 30 seconds and reinforce inside corners with thin coils of soft clay.
over three to four days. Apply three coats of PVA inside and two outside. Paint or leave natural. Use for dry-soil plants only.
Press horizontal texture lines into the wall panels before assembly to suggest stacked stone or bark. Group all three planters at different heights on a windowsill.

items.problem: Panel corners gap at the top during drying
items.cause: Clay at the vertical joints dried and contracted at slightly different rates, opening the join at the top where there is no base to hold the angle
items.fix: Bind the outside of the assembled planter with a loose rubber band while leather-hard to hold the walls together. Remove the band before bone-dry so it does not cut into the clay

items.problem: Hexagonal base does not match the wall perimeter
items.cause: The base was cut slightly smaller or larger than the wall assembly
items.fix: Score and slip the base edge and press it up against the wall assembly from below, trimming any overhang with the fettling knife before the clay dries
